textRun.content: Retrieval Accelerates but Does Not Replace Few-Shot Adaptation of Visual Inverse Dynamics: An Action-Error–Compute Benchmark on LIBERO-Goal
Working manuscript | Protocol v6 with frozen final-analysis amendment 1b42ba59 | Revised 18 October 2026

Video-planning robot controllers translate a predicted future frame into actions with an inverse-dynamics model (IDM). When a new task supplies only a few demonstrations, the IDM must adapt, and the cost of that adaptation matters alongside its accuracy. We study few-shot IDM adaptation on held-out LIBERO-Goal tasks and measure action error (chunk mean-squared error on normalized actions, and R²) against adaptation compute (GPU-seconds and FLOPs per update). Our method, RAID, is a retrieval-augmented IDM whose head attends over 16 support transitions retrieved in a frozen reference space and gates the resulting prior against a direct prediction. We compare it with nine re-implemented baselines covering nearest-neighbour action regression, retrieve-and-blend prediction, retrieved training data, head-only and full fine-tuning, LoRA, and frozen-encoder probes. After development on two tasks, we froze the method set, comparisons and decision rule, and then ran once on two sealed tasks with three seeds. Without target training, RAID was worse than VINN-style k-nearest-neighbour regression (MSE 0.500 vs 0.376), so the first frozen comparison failed. After 25 updates, RAID with LoRA (0.272) had lower error than all nine baselines in all six task–seed settings. After 500 updates it showed no clear difference from head-only, LoRA and probe baselines and was worse than full fine-tuning (0.268). An exploratory frozen-encoder variant of RAID reached LoRA's 500-update error after about 0.14 GPU-seconds, whereas LoRA needed about 190. A post hoc analysis links the zero-training failure to one task on which the source-trained direct prediction is far outside its usual error range and the learned gate does not fall back to retrieval. A 40-episode closed-loop pilot with a frozen video generator yields low success for all conditions (0–2 of 10) and is reported only as secondary evidence. Retrieval therefore accelerates, but does not replace, few-shot IDM adaptation.
inverse dynamics; few-shot adaptation; retrieval; LoRA; adaptation compute; visual planning; robot learning.

Visual world models make possible futures available as images or video, but a visual proposal must still be translated into executable robot actions. UniPi connects text-conditioned video planning with a separately trained inverse-dynamics model [
]. More recent systems retain this decomposition: π0.7 conditions a generalist controller on visual subgoals [
], OpenWAM supports composable visual-prediction and inverse-dynamics components [
], and GE-Act 2.0 and VPP2 couple a visual planner with an action module [

]. When the visual predictor stays fixed, task-specific knowledge must enter through the action-inference component. This paper studies how that component, an inverse-dynamics model (IDM) that maps the current observation, robot state and a target future frame to an action chunk, should adapt to a new task from five demonstrations.
With few target demonstrations, an IDM can use the demonstrations at prediction time, as in nearest-neighbour regression and retrieval-augmented policies [
]; it can use them to select additional training data [
]; or it can update parameters, from an action head alone to low-rank adapters [

] and full fine-tuning. These options differ sharply in cost. Retrieval needs no target training but adds lookup at inference. Head-only training on cached frozen features is cheap. LoRA and full fine-tuning run the image encoder at every update. Comparisons that report only accuracy after a fixed number of updates hide this difference.

We therefore treat few-shot IDM adaptation as a measurement problem: action error on held-out recorded transitions as a function of adaptation compute. The primary metric is chunk mean-squared error on normalized actions, averaged over query demonstrations, together with R²; compute is measured in adaptation GPU-seconds, FLOPs per update, trainable parameters and per-decision cost. Task success is secondary evidence. End-to-end few-shot policies are much stronger on success: in DISC's five-demonstration LIBERO-Goal evaluation, reported success at the best checkpoint is 55.0% for Octo, 68.5% for VQ-BeT and 73.0% for DISC [
], under a protocol different from ours. Our closed-loop pilot reaches at most 2 of 10 episodes. We do not compete on task success, and offline action error is not a substitute for it.

Our method, RAID (Retrieval-Augmented Inverse Dynamics), retrieves the 16 support transitions closest to the query in a frozen reference representation. A learned head attends over the retrieved action chunks and mixes the resulting prior with a direct prediction through a per-dimension gate. Retrieval keys always come from the frozen reference encoder, so adapting the controller encoder with LoRA never changes the geometry of the support bank. Neither retrieval combined with LoRA nor a new world–action-model architecture is a sufficient novelty claim: ReCAP adds trajectory retrieval to a frozen world–action policy [
], HAND retrieves robot experience and then fine-tunes a policy [
], and VLA-Pro retrieves and fuses task-specific LoRA adapters [
]. Our contribution is a controlled measurement of when retrieval helps an adapting IDM and what it costs.

The protocol separates design from evaluation. All method development used two development tasks. We then froze the method set, comparisons, interval method and decision rule in a digest-bound amendment before any final-task file was read, and ran the frozen benchmark once on two sealed final tasks with three seeds. Two of our variants were designed after development results were known; development data were therefore used for design, but final-task data were not. Throughout,
: the final tasks are held out from our training and design, but we make no claim that LIBERO is unseen by the pretrained models in the pipeline.
A compute-aware few-shot IDM benchmark on LIBERO-Goal.

Fifteen methods, six training-free and nine trained, are evaluated on the same support sets, query transitions, normalizers and update schedule, and each trained method yields an error-versus-GPU-second curve. The nine baselines are re-implementations of established method families in our setting, not reproductions of the published systems.

Video planning followed by action inference has substantial precedent. UniPi uses a separately trained inverse model [
]. π0.7 employs visual subgoal conditioning, treats the resulting action prediction as an inverse-dynamics-like problem, and trains with both real and generated subgoals [
]. OpenWAM defines local dynamics interfaces from the current observation, proprioception and a supplied future, and studies reuse of an inverse model with adapted visual predictors [
]. GE-Act 2.0 connects visual planning and inverse dynamics with an explicit mechanism for aligning generated futures with action supervision [
], and VPP2 distills a video model into a visual planner with an action module [
]. Other world–action models couple video and actions more tightly: DreamZero models them jointly [
], and Cosmos 3 supports several visual and action input–output configurations [
]. Fast-WAM questions whether test-time future imagination is needed at all [
], and RoboWM-Bench and EVA judge visual predictions through execution rather than appearance [
]. Inverse dynamics also supports learning from observation [
] and policy supervision from synthetic video [
]; its label efficiency depends on the setting [
]. We fix the visual predictor and study only how the IDM adapts.
VINN separates representation learning from behavior learning and predicts actions by locally weighted nearest-neighbour regression [

]. REGENT retrieves demonstrations and combines them with a learned transformer policy, including a retrieve-and-play baseline and a distance-weighted interpolation between the retrieved action and the model output, so that it can act in new environments without mandatory fine-tuning [
]. RT-Cache retrieves and replays action snippets from visual memory [
], CLAW maps latent actions to executable controls through nearest-neighbour lookup [
], and RAEA integrates retrieved experience through cross-attention [
]. ReCAP adds trajectory retrieval to Cosmos Policy and extends task coverage by adding demonstrations while the policy stays frozen [

]. Our training-free baselines re-implement three of these mechanisms: VINN-style weighted k-NN, REGENT retrieve-and-play and a REGENT-style blend. RAID differs in that a learned head selects among retrieved candidates and gates them against a direct prediction, and in that we combine it with target-time parameter updates inside a separate IDM.
Retrieval can also select training data. Behavior Retrieval queries unlabeled prior data for few-shot imitation [
], FlowRetrieval uses optical flow to guide retrieval [
], STRAP retrieves sub-trajectories to augment policy training [
], and importance-weighted retrieval corrects the retrieval distribution [
]. HAND retrieves robot experience by hand path and fine-tunes a policy on it [
]. Our STRAP-style baseline mixes support transitions with their nearest source-task transitions during head training; retrieval then affects only the training data, not the prediction.
LoRA freezes the original weights and learns an additive low-rank update [
]. TAIL evaluates LoRA and other lightweight adapters for continual robot imitation [
], and FADA adapts inverse dynamics behind a frozen planner [
]; our LoRA baseline follows this family. OpenVLA studies efficient policy fine-tuning [
], and OpenVLA-OFT shows that action representation, chunking, decoding and the training objective affect both performance and inference cost [
], which motivates measuring resources rather than counting parameters alone. WIZARD [

] investigate other adaptation mechanisms; VLA-Pro in particular retrieves and fuses LoRA adapters, whereas RAID retrieves labeled visual transitions. RoboTTT uses test-time learning over robot context [
], and retrieval/fine-tuning hybrids also appear in language-model-based world modeling [
]. These precedents rule out a broad novelty claim for combining memory and parameter updates.
Pretrained encoders supply the representation for inverse dynamics. MAE learns image features through masked reconstruction [
], R3M studies frozen representations for manipulation [
], and VC-1 shows that frozen-representation quality varies across embodied tasks and adaptation settings [

]. Our frozen-encoder probe (a freshly initialized head on frozen MAE features) and head-only fine-tuning belong to this protocol family. We also distinguish the controller representation, which LoRA may change, from the frozen reference representation used for retrieval keys and queries.

End-to-end policies adapt an entire visuomotor policy and report task success. DISC generates task-specific policy parameters from instructions and, in its five-demonstration LIBERO-Goal evaluation, reports success at checkpoints between 50 and 1,000 adaptation steps of 15.5–68.5% for VQ-BeT, 16.0–55.0% for Octo and 60.0–73.0% for DISC, with Diffusion Policy at or below 1.5% [

]. These numbers come from a different task split, pretraining set and evaluation protocol and are not matched baselines. We cite them to position our work: we study the IDM component of a modular pipeline and its adaptation cost, and we make no claim of competitive task success.
LIBERO-Goal contains ten tasks that share objects and layout but differ in their goals, with 50 demonstrations each [

]. We use a fixed split into six source tasks, two development tasks and two final tasks (Appendix A, Table A1). For each target task, 30 demonstrations form a support pool and 20 form the query set. A support seed s ∈ {42, 43, 44} selects K = 5 support demonstrations from the pool; the same seed also seeds source training. One (task, seed) pair is a
; each stage has 2 tasks × 3 seeds = 6 settings.

At time t the IDM receives the current RGB observation oₜ, the future observation oₜ₊ₕ with H = 8, the current proprioception qₜ (7 joint positions and 2 gripper positions, normalized with source-training statistics) and the requested duration H. It predicts an action chunk âₜ:ₜ₊₇ ∈ ℝ^{8×7} in the LIBERO action convention, normalized per dimension with source-training statistics.

Every stride-1 window of each query demonstration is evaluated with the recorded future frame oₜ₊₈ and its logged action chunk. The error of a window is the mean squared error over the 56 normalized action elements. Errors are averaged within each query demonstration, then over the 20 query demonstrations (macro average); we report the mean over the six settings. R² is the mean over the seven action dimensions of 1 − SSE/SST over all query chunk elements. Because the future frame is recorded, this setting measures action inference given a correct future and is not affected by generator quality.

For each trained method we record the error after n ∈ {0, 25, 50, 100, 200, 350, 500} updates and the cumulative adaptation GPU-seconds C(n): synchronized wall-clock time of the updates on one GPU, excluding evaluation. We also record FLOPs per update (forward and backward pass, batch 64), trainable parameters, and the latency, FLOPs and peak memory of one control decision at batch size 1. One-time costs shared by all methods (source training and the frozen feature cache) are reported separately and are not included in C(n).

A frozen video generator receives the current RGB frame and the instruction and returns a clip; the IDM converts frames of that clip into action chunks that are executed in the simulator. The outcome is unfiltered task success. Logged actions from a different trajectory are not ground truth for an arbitrary generated future, so closed-loop success and offline error answer different questions.

The pipeline has a frozen visual generator and an IDM. The generator is conditioned only on the current RGB frame and the instruction; recorded futures, logged actions, privileged simulator state and native generator actions are excluded from the controller input. In the offline benchmark the generator is not used. In the closed-loop pilot it is the standalone Stage-1 video model of VPP2 [
], pinned to a fixed repository commit; earlier feasibility tests with Cosmos3-Edge [
] are not part of the reported results.
4.2 Controller, frozen reference retrieval and source training
The controller encoder φ is an MAE ViT-B/16 [

]; its 768-dimensional normalized CLS features of oₜ and oₜ₊ₕ, together with qₜ and H, form the state s. A separate frozen copy φ_ref produces the retrieval keys and queries. A support bank stores, for every support window, φ_ref(oₜ), φ_ref(oₜ₊ₕ), qₜ, H, the normalized action chunk and the parent demonstration. The retrieval distance is
d = 0.5 (1 − cos(φ_ref(oₜ), φ_ref(o′ₜ))) + 0.5 (1 − cos(φ_ref(oₜ₊ₕ), φ_ref(o′ₜ₊ₕ))) + 0.1 · mean((qₜ − q′ₜ)²),
with exact duration matching; similarity is −d. Because keys are always computed with φ_ref, controller adaptation cannot invalidate the bank.

One source controller per head type and seed is trained on the six source tasks (40 training, 5 validation and 5 retention demonstrations per task) for 2,000 updates with batch 64, AdamW (learning rate 3·10⁻⁴, weight decay 10⁻⁴) and gradient clipping at 1.0. The objective averages a retrieval-present loss and a masked-memory (null-retrieval) loss with equal weight. For the retrieval-present term, each query retrieves from an episodic bank of 2, 5 or 10 demonstrations of the same source task, excluding the query's own demonstration. The checkpoint with the lowest source-validation error, evaluated every 100 updates, is kept.
4.3 RAID v6: retrieval block and MLP

RAID v6 appends a fixed-width retrieval block to the controller input: four similarity-sorted neighbour slots, each holding a normalized action chunk, its similarity and a validity flag, followed by their softmax-weighted mean (temperature 0.1). Missing neighbours are masked, and an empty bank yields a finite null block. A three-layer MLP (hidden widths 512 and 256, LayerNorm, ReLU, dropout 0.1) maps the input to the action chunk.
4.4 RAID v7: attention over retrieved candidates with a per-dimension gate
RAID v7 retrieves k = 16 candidates with the same frozen-reference distance and computes
αᵢ = softmax_i( (W_q s) · (W_k [φ̂_ref(oⁱₜ), φ̂_ref(oⁱₜ₊ₕ), simᵢ]) / √128 ) over valid candidates,

where f_θ is the MLP trunk of §4.3, φ̂ denotes L2-normalized features, aⁱ is the normalized action chunk of candidate i, and the gate is set to g = 1 when no candidate is valid (null memory). During training, Gaussian noise with standard deviation 0.05 is added to candidate actions. An auxiliary selection loss pulls attention toward candidates whose actions match the target,
L_sel = KL(w* ‖ α), w*ᵢ ∝ exp(−mse(aⁱ, a)), restricted to valid candidates,

applied with weight 0.1 when at least two candidates are valid, both in source training and in adaptation. Retrieval enters the head as candidate keys and values rather than as a fixed input block, so the head can learn which candidates to trust and, through the gate, how much to trust retrieval at all.

All trained methods use the same five support demonstrations, normalizers, 500-update schedule, batch size 64, sampler seed stream, optimizer settings (AdamW; head learning rate 3·10⁻⁴; adapter learning rate 10⁻⁴; weight decay 10⁻⁴; gradient clip 1.0) and checkpoints.
Rank-8, α = 16 LoRA (dropout 0) on the qkv and output projections of MAE blocks 10 and 11, plus the source-trained head; the adapter is inserted with zero initial effect. LoRA receives null memory.

The same LoRA and head updates with retrieval active during adaptation and evaluation. During adaptation, each support query excludes its entire parent demonstration from the bank, so it retrieves from the other four demonstrations; at evaluation it retrieves from all five. Controller features come from the LoRA-adapted encoder and retrieval keys from φ_ref, so each decision needs two image encodings. RAID+LoRA v6 and RAID+LoRA v7 differ only in the head.

The encoder stays frozen and features are cached. Only the RAID v7 head (trunk, attention and gate; 1,420,832 parameters) is trained, with the same retrieval exclusion and the same schedule and sample stream as head-only fine-tuning. This variant was defined after the development results were known.

he VINN-style baseline uses the frozen MAE reference space rather than VINN's own self-supervised encoder. The STRAP-style baseline retrieves the four nearest source-task windows for every support window from the training demonstrations of all six source tasks, in the frozen reference space, and fills half of each batch with these retrieved windows.

Each setting evaluates every method on the 20 query demonstrations of one target task with recorded future frames. Trained methods are evaluated at all seven checkpoints. Source controllers are bitwise identical across runs with the same seed: an exploratory rerun reproduced the training-free methods and every head-only checkpoint of the earlier development run exactly (largest per-demonstration difference 0.0), which allows the exploratory RAID v7 head-only results to be paired with that run.

All methods of a run share one GPU and 16 CPU threads. Adaptation GPU-seconds exclude evaluation, and FLOPs are counted with PyTorch's FLOP counter. Decision cost is measured at batch size 1 and includes encoding the current and future frames, a second encoding with φ_ref when the controller encoder is adapted and retrieval is active, retrieval, and the head. On the final run (NVIDIA A100-SXM4-80GB), the one-time reference feature cache took 119 s, and source training took 279–301 s per head type and seed for 2,000 updates. These shared costs are excluded from C(n); they exceed the entire adaptation cost of the frozen-encoder methods by two orders of magnitude but are amortized across target tasks. Development benchmarks ran on different A100 variants, so we compare GPU-seconds only within a run.
5.4 Development, frozen plan and final run

Development used only the two development tasks: a compute-aware benchmark of v6 and v7 (16–17 October 2026), the nine-baseline benchmark (17 October), and the exploratory RAID v7 head-only run (17 October). On 17 October 2026 at 20:15 UTC, before any final-task data were hashed, packaged or read, we froze an analysis amendment (SHA-256 digest 1b42ba59…) that fixes the method set, metrics, checkpoints and the following comparisons:
RAID v7 without training versus the best training-free baseline on development data (VINN-style k-NN, development MSE 0.426).

the RAID variant with the lowest development error at each budget versus each of the nine baselines, at 25 and at 500 updates. The rule selected RAID+LoRA v7 at both budgets (development MSE 0.308 and 0.290).
error at fixed budgets of 0.1, 0.5, 1, 10 and 100 GPU-seconds (last checkpoint within the budget), and GPU-seconds to reach LoRA's 500-update error.

For each comparison we compute the paired difference (ours minus baseline) per query demonstration. The primary 95% interval is a percentile bootstrap over the six task × seed clusters (10,000 resamples, seed 0); we also report a demonstration-level interval and the number of settings won out of six. The decision rule is
if the cluster interval lies entirely below zero,
otherwise. No multiplicity correction is applied. With only six clusters, a percentile bootstrap can be too narrow, so the interval should be read together with settings won.

The final run evaluated the two sealed tasks with seeds 42, 43 and 44 once. Its package contained only source and final tasks, final-task access was gated by the frozen amendment, and nothing was tuned afterwards. The final stage has been used and will not be rerun.

The closed-loop pilot preceded the v7 design and therefore evaluates the four original conditions: frozen source controller, RAID v6, LoRA and RAID+LoRA v6. It used the two development tasks, seed 42 and five recorded initial states per task, giving 40 episodes. For each plan, VPP2 generated one clip from the current frame and a structured scene prompt written by a language model (two candidate prompts and a language-model judge); frames 9 and 18 of the clip served as targets for two 8-step chunks before replanning from the condition's own observation, up to 300 steps. The first plan of each case was shared by all four conditions. We waived a planned 15-case human-rating gate for generated clips on 14 October 2026, before the first pilot episode. The decision followed a five-case panel in which 5/5 clips were technically valid and 3/5 selected clips were judged acceptable, but the registered timing rule failed (median frame offset 3, threshold 4); the generator's timing calibration therefore remained weak. Success is the simulator's task check.

fter 25 updates, RAID+LoRA v7 reached 0.272 and was better than all nine baselines in all six settings, with every cluster interval below zero (Table 5; Figure 2). The margins over the strongest trained baselines were moderate: −0.049 against head-only fine-tuning, −0.044 against LoRA and −0.042 against full fine-tuning. After 500 updates, the advantage disappeared. RAID+LoRA v7 (0.281) showed no clear difference from head-only fine-tuning, LoRA, LoRA without source training and the frozen-encoder probe; it was worse than full fine-tuning (+0.013, [+0.004, +0.021], 1/6), which had the lowest error of all methods (0.268); and it remained better than the STRAP-style baseline and all training-free baselines. Its error curve was not monotone: the minimum occurred at 25 updates, and later checkpoints were between 0.280 and 0.291. The frozen protocol used a fixed schedule without early stopping, because selecting a checkpoint on final-task error was not allowed.

Two secondary comparisons support the role of the v7 head (FINAL_RESULTS.md, "Secondary comparisons"). RAID+LoRA v6 had no clear advantage over LoRA at 25 updates (−0.018, [−0.042, +0.001], 3/6) and was worse at 500 updates (+0.052, [+0.043, +0.063], 0/6). The exploratory RAID v7 head-only was better than LoRA at 25 updates (−0.042, [−0.059, −0.027], 6/6) and showed no clear difference at 500 updates (+0.004, [−0.002, +0.011], 2/6).

igure 3 plots error against adaptation GPU-seconds. Methods that keep the encoder frozen reach low error within about one GPU-second, because each update touches only the head on cached features (0.3–1.2 GFLOP per update). LoRA-based methods run the image encoder at every update (about 5.2 TFLOP per update) and need tens to hundreds of seconds; full fine-tuning needs 13.6 TFLOP per update but reaches the lowest error at 100 s (0.266). The exploratory RAID v7 head-only reached 0.273 at its first checkpoint (25 updates, 0.14 GPU-s), below LoRA's 500-update error of 0.283; LoRA itself reaches that error only at its last checkpoint, after about 187 GPU-seconds. Retrieval therefore buys a large reduction in the compute needed for a given error at small budgets.

Figure 3. Mean chunk MSE on the final tasks against cumulative adaptation GPU-seconds (symmetric log scale; zero means no training). Markers are the checkpoints at 0, 25, 50, 100, 200, 350 and 500 updates. Shared one-time costs (feature cache, source training) are excluded.

This per-second advantage is not consistent across stages. On development tasks, plain head-only fine-tuning was better than RAID v7 head-only at every fixed budget, because one head-only update costs about 2.4 ms and one RAID v7 head update about 6 ms (V7HEAD_RESULTS.md); neither reached LoRA's development 500-update error. The robust statement is that the RAID head improves error per update; per GPU-second it is comparable to plain head-only training.

Retrieval has an inference cost. At batch size 1, every method except RAID+LoRA needed 6.8–7.5 ms and about 70 GFLOP per decision. RAID+LoRA v6 and v7 needed 13.9–14.0 ms and 141 GFLOP, because they encode each frame twice (adapted controller features and frozen retrieval keys). The frozen-encoder RAID v7 head-only needs a single encoding (7.5 ms).
6.4 Post hoc analysis of the zero-training failure

This analysis was not part of the frozen plan. It was performed after the final results were known, changes no frozen result, and uses only the collected per-demonstration errors of the six final and six development settings. Gate values, attention weights and retrieval distances were not saved, so statements about the gate are inferences from errors, not measurements.

The failure is specific to one task. On the wine-bottle task, VINN-style k-NN over the same support bank still performed as on other tasks (0.406), whereas both learned RAID heads failed (RAID v6 0.692, RAID v7 0.682; R² of RAID v7 −0.51). The frozen source controller's error on this task (1.453) was far above its error on the other three held-out tasks (0.630–0.882).

On this task, RAID v7 errors followed the source controller rather than retrieval (Figure 4). Across its 60 query demonstrations (3 seeds × 20), the Pearson correlation between RAID v7 and frozen-source errors was 0.97 (Spearman 0.95), whereas the correlation with k-NN errors was 0.31 (Spearman 0.26), and RAID v7 was worse than k-NN on 92% of the demonstrations. Figure 4 shows the per-demonstration errors. On the other three tasks, RAID v7 errors correlated more strongly with k-NN errors (Pearson 0.77–0.91) than with source errors (0.62–0.78), and RAID v7 was worse than k-NN on 38–50% of demonstrations.

The failure appeared only when the source controller was far outside its usual range. In the nine other settings, frozen-source error ranged from 0.56 to 0.96 and RAID v7 minus k-NN from −0.074 to +0.016; in the three wine-bottle settings, frozen-source error ranged from 1.38 to 1.52 and RAID v7 minus k-NN from +0.208 to +0.363. With one failing task, this pattern cannot establish a threshold rule.

A few target updates repaired the failure. After 25 updates, RAID+LoRA v7 had the lowest error of head-only, LoRA and RAID+LoRA v7 on every task, and its largest margin over LoRA was on the wine-bottle task (0.287 vs 0.348).

Our interpretation is that the zero-training RAID heads depend on the source-trained direct path: when that path is badly wrong for a new task, the learned gate does not fall back to retrieval, whereas k-NN has no such dependence. Why the source controller fails on this task was not tested. One hypothesis is interference from the source task "put the wine bottle on the rack", which shares the object but not the goal.

uccess was low for all conditions: 3 successes in 40 episodes, all other episodes timing out at 300 steps. The registered descriptive contrasts were +0.2 for RAID+LoRA over RAID, +0.1 over LoRA, and an interaction of +0.1. The two RAID+LoRA successes and the single LoRA success occurred on different starts, so the paired difference between them was +1 on two cases and −1 on one. With this sample, no difference is statistically meaningful. Offline, on the same pilot support sets, LoRA had the lowest action error (0.341 and 0.225 on the two tasks) and RAID+LoRA v6 the second lowest (0.420 and 0.285), so the offline and closed-loop rankings did not agree. Generated and executed videos are retained (Appendix C).

Retrieved support actions act as a strong prior that makes few updates sufficient: with 25 updates, both RAID v7 variants (0.272 and 0.273) reached lower error than head-only fine-tuning, LoRA and the frozen-encoder probe after 500 updates; only full fine-tuning was lower (0.268). With enough updates, parameter adaptation alone reaches about the same error, and full fine-tuning, the most expensive method, is best. Retrieval therefore changes the cost of reaching a given error rather than the error that is ultimately reachable in this setting.
Why learned retrieval failed without training.

The training-free result reversed between development and final tasks. The post hoc analysis suggests that a learned gate inherits the failures of the source-trained direct path, whereas plain k-NN does not. A gate that depends on retrieval confidence or on the disagreement between the direct prediction and the retrieved actions could allow a fallback to retrieval. Such a change must be designed on development tasks and tested on new held-out tasks under a new frozen plan, because the current final tasks have been used.

Frozen-encoder methods are the cheapest to adapt, by two orders of magnitude, but depend on a one-time feature cache and source training that cost several minutes. RAID+LoRA doubles the per-decision cost through its second encoding. A deployment that adapts once and acts many times may prefer a different trade-off from one that adapts for every new task.
The primary evidence is offline action error with recorded futures. It does not measure task success, and it does not measure robustness to imperfect generated futures.
The final evaluation has two tasks and three seeds. The cluster bootstrap rests on six clusters and can be too narrow; no multiplicity correction is applied across the 19 frozen comparisons.
RAID v7 and RAID v7 head-only were designed after development results were known. The final tasks were not used for design, but the design is not independent of the development tasks.
The baselines are re-implementations with our encoder, inputs and schedule. They do not represent the published systems, and other hyperparameters could change their ranking.
A single encoder (MAE ViT-B/16), one LoRA configuration, one benchmark suite and one support size (K = 5) were evaluated.

The closed-loop pilot is small (40 episodes, one seed), evaluates the v6 heads only, used a generator whose timing calibration was weak, and ran after we waived a human-rating gate on the basis of a five-case panel.
We cannot verify that the pretrained models in the pipeline never saw LIBERO;
GPU-seconds depend on hardware and implementation; the comparisons are valid within a run on one GPU.

On held-out LIBERO-Goal tasks with five demonstrations, retrieval-augmented inverse dynamics reduced the adaptation compute needed for a given action error but did not lower the error reachable with enough updates. Under a plan frozen before the final data were read, RAID+LoRA v7 was better than all nine re-implemented baselines after 25 updates (0.272, 6/6 settings), showed no clear difference from most of them after 500 updates, and was worse than full fine-tuning (0.268). Without any training, the learned retrieval head failed against plain k-NN (0.500 vs 0.376) because of one task on which the source controller was far out of range. These results are offline, rest on two final tasks, and do not establish task success, broad generalization or real-world transfer.
